extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or graduate students studying measure theory and Lebesgue integration
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted material treats product measures, Fubini's Theorem, measurability of sections, integration of complex- and vector-valued functions, and the construction/properties of L^1, L^2, and L^∞ spaces. It is a textbook-level presentation with definitions, lemmas, propositions, proofs, and remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone class definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A class of sets is called a monotone class if it is closed under countable increasing unions and countable decreasing intersections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intersection of any nonempty family of monotone classes is a monotone class, so there is a smallest monotone class containing any given class of sets. Notation ↑ and ↓ denote increasing countable union and decreasing countable intersection respectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone Class Lemma (Lemma 5.43)
rubrics_metrics.description: The smallest monotone class containing an algebra M is identical to the smallest σ-algebra A containing M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline: show the monotone class containing M is closed under finite union and complementation (hence under countable unions), using three steps: closure under intersections with fixed A, closure under finite unions, and closure under complements; this justifies using monotone-class arguments to promote algebraic identities to full σ-algebras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurability of section integrals for sets (Lemma 5.44)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X,A,µ) and (Y,B,ν) are σ-finite measure spaces, then for every E in A×B the functions x ↦ ν(E_x) and y ↦ µ(E^y) are measurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: let M be the class of sets E for which the section-integral functions are measurable; show M is a monotone class containing the algebra of finite disjoint unions of rectangles, then apply the Monotone Class Lemma. Uses additivity and monotone convergence and reduction from finite to σ-finite via partitioning into finite-measure pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product measure existence and uniqueness (Proposition 5.45)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given σ-finite measure spaces (X,A,µ) and (Y,B,ν) there exists a unique measure µ×ν on A×B such that µ×ν(A×B)=µ(A)ν(B) for rectangles A×B. The product measure is σ-finite and for every E in A×B, (µ×ν)(E)=∫_X ν(E_x) dµ(x)=∫_Y µ(E^y) dν(y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: define ρ(E)=∫_X ν(E_x) dµ(x) (measurability of ν(E_x) is used); show ρ is completely additive on the algebra of finite disjoint unions of rectangles and σ-finite; extend by the Extension Theorem to the σ-algebra generated by rectangles; symmetry gives the other iterated integral equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections of measurable functions are measurable (Lemma 5.46)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is a measurable function on the product space X×Y, then for each fixed x in X the function y ↦ f(x,y) is measurable on Y, and for each fixed y in Y the function x ↦ f(x,y) is measurable on X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: level sets {y : f(x,y) > c} are sections of measurable sets in X×Y, hence measurable by Proposition 5.42; similarly for fixed y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fubini's Theorem for nonnegative functions (Theorem 5.47)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let (X,A,µ) and (Y,B,ν) be σ-finite measure spaces. If f is a nonnegative measurable function on X×Y, then x ↦ ∫_Y f(x,y) dν(y) and y ↦ ∫_X f(x,y) dµ(x) are measurable and ∫_{X×Y} f d(µ×ν) = ∫_X (∫_Y f(x,y) dν(y)) dµ(x) = ∫_Y (∫_X f(x,y) dµ(x)) dν(y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: check for indicator functions (Proposition 5.45), extend to simple functions, then approximate arbitrary nonnegative measurable f by an increasing sequence of simple functions and apply the Monotone Convergence Theorem repeatedly to justify exchanging limits and integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero-measure sections corollary (Corollary 5.48)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E ⊆ X×Y is measurable and for almost every x (dµ) the x-section E_x has ν-measure 0, then for almost every y (dν) the y-section E^y has µ-measure 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Just apply Fubini's Theorem to the indicator function I_E: one iterated integral is 0 by hypothesis, so the other must also be 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fubini for integrable (signed/complex) functions — absolute integrability hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is measurable on X×Y and one of the iterated integrals of |f| (∫_X (∫_Y |f(x,y)| dν(y)) dµ(x) or ∫_Y (∫_X |f(x,y)| dµ(x)) dν(y)) is finite, then: (a) f is integrable on X×Y; (b) for a.e. x the inner integral ∫_Y f(x,y) dν(y) is defined and (after redefining on a null set) is measurable and integrable over X; (c) similarly for the other order; (d) the double integral equals each iterated integral and the two iterated integrals are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is proved by applying Fubini to the positive and negative parts f^+ and f^- separately. The needed 'redeﬁnitions on null sets' ensure pointwise-defined integrands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat about completions and product σ-algebras
rubrics_metrics.description: The completion of A×B (the σ-algebra on the product) need not equal the product of the completions of A and B; accordingly, statements of Fubini require modification when using completions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Euclidean space it's preferable where possible to work with Borel sets; Lebesgue measurable sets in product spaces may misbehave under product formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurability criterion for complex/vector-valued functions (Lemma 5.49, Prop. 5.50, 5.51)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : X → C^m is measurable iff the inverse image under f of every open set in C^m lies in A. Equivalently, Re f and Im f are measurable (Proposition 5.50). Equivalently, (f, v) is measurable for each v in C^m; it suffices to check (f, u_j) for the standard basis u_j (Proposition 5.51).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives both 'strong' measurability (inverse images of opens) and 'weak' measurability (scalar inner products) and shows their equivalence in finite dimensions. Use basic-open-set decomposition and coordinate functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic/closure properties of measurable vector-valued functions (Proposition 5.52)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f,g : X → C^m are measurable then f+g and scalar multiples c f are measurable; conjugation ¯f is measurable; products (f,v) etc. are measurable; pointwise limits of measurable sequences are measurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs reduce to continuity of coordinate-wise algebraic operations and application of previous measurability equivalences; reduces many vector-valued measurability facts to the scalar case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability of complex-valued functions (definition and properties, Proposition 5.53)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex-valued function f is integrable on E if Re f and Im f are integrable on E; in that case ∫_E f dµ = ∫_E Re f dµ + i ∫_E Im f dµ. Linearity, scalar multiplication, dominated convergence, and the real-valued integrability criterion (|f| integrable implies f integrable) hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dominated convergence and linearity are proved by applying the corresponding real-valued theorems separately to Re f and Im f. Multiplying by unit complex constants can be used to reduce to real integrals when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability of finite-dimensional vector-valued functions (definition and properties, Proposition 5.54)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : X → C^m is integrable on E iff each scalar function (f, u_j) (inner product with standard basis vectors) is integrable; define ∫_E f dµ componentwise. Properties: linearity, scalar multiplication, (f,v) integrable for fixed v with ∫(f,v)= (∫f, v), dominated convergence, and a norm-dominated integrability criterion (if |f(x)| ≤ g(x) with integrable g then f integrable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition reduces vector integrability to integrability of scalar components; dominated convergence and other properties follow by componentwise application of the scalar results and Schwarz inequality for estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of L^1, L^2, L^∞ via pseudonorms and essential supremum
rubrics_metrics.description: For measurable scalar functions define pseudonorms: ||f||_1 = ∫ |f| dµ, ||f||_2 = (∫ |f|^2 dµ)^{1/2}, and ||f||_∞ = ess sup |f| (the infimum of essential bounds). The vector spaces V of measurable functions with finite pseudonorm become pseudo-normed linear spaces; quotienting by functions equal a.e. yields the normed spaces L^1(X), L^2(X), and L^∞(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential supremum is the infimum of M such that |f|≤M almost everywhere; the equivalence-class construction addresses that pseudonorm can be zero for nonzero functions on null sets. One may abuse notation and speak of 'f∈L^p' treating representatives as functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density of simple/indicator functions in L^p (Proposition 5.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every indicator function of a set of finite measure lies in L^p for p=1 or 2. The smallest closed subspace of L^p containing all such indicators is L^p itself (hence simple functions built from finite-measure sets are dense in L^1 and L^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: approximate nonnegative L^p functions by increasing simple functions and use dominated/monotone convergence to approximate in norm; note density in L^∞ holds iff µ(X) is finite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of normed linear spaces and bounded linear operators (Propositions 5.55 and 5.57)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any normed linear space addition and scalar multiplication are continuous, the closure of any vector subspace is a vector subspace, and finite linear combinations of a subset S are dense in the smallest closed subspace generated by S. For a linear operator L between normed spaces, the following are equivalent: uniform continuity, continuity, continuity at 0, and boundedness (existence of M with ||Lx|| ≤ M||x||). The operator norm is the infimum of such M and equals sup_{||x||≤1} ||Lx||.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These topological/functional-analytic facts are used to handle completeness, density, continuity, and operator bounds in L^p spaces; proofs use basic norm inequalities and linearity.
